nodes.summary: Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be profiles, each assigning a strict total order on the alternatives to every voter, and let $i$ be a voter. Then $p_2$ differs from $p_1$ at most at voter $i$ when $p_1(j) = p_2(j)$ for every voter $j \ne i$.
nodes.title: Profiles differing only at one voter

nodes.summary: Let the set of alternatives be finite and the set of voters be finite and nonempty, and suppose there are at least three distinct alternatives. Then every resolute social choice function on profiles of strict preference orders that is onto and strategy-proof is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem, finiteness form

nodes.summary: Let the set of alternatives be finite and the set of voters be finite and nonempty, and suppose there are at least three distinct alternatives. Then every resolute social choice function on profiles of strict preference orders that is onto and strategy-proof is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a type $\alpha$, with relation $\lt _T$. Then $a \lt _T a$ fails for every $a \in \alpha$.
nodes.title: Irreflexivity of strict preference

nodes.summary: For a resolute social choice function $F$, a voter $d$ is a dictator when, for every profile $p$, the chosen alternative $F(p)$ is top-ranked in the preference order $p(d)$ of voter $d$.
nodes.title: Dictator of a social choice function

nodes.summary: A resolute social choice function $F$ is dictatorial when some voter is a dictator for $F$: there is a voter $d$ such that, for every profile $p$, the chosen alternative $F(p)$ is top-ranked in the preference order $p(d)$ of voter $d$.
nodes.title: Dictatorial social choice function

nodes.summary: A resolute social choice function $F$ is onto when every alternative $a$ is chosen at some profile, that is, $F(p) = a$ for some profile $p$.
nodes.title: Onto social choice function

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $P$, write $x \succ_P y$ when $x$ is related to $y$ by $P$ ($P$ ranks $x$ above $y$). A resolute social choice function $F$ is strategy-proof when, for all profiles $p_1$, $p_2$ and every voter $i$ such that $p_1(j) = p_2(j)$ for all voters $j \ne i$, it is not the case that $F(p_2) \succ_{p_1(i)} F(p_1)$: no voter gains by misreporting alone, judged by the true order $p_1(i)$.
nodes.title: Strategy-proof social choice function

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $o$ on the alternatives, write $x \succ_o y$ when $x$ is related to $y$ by $o$ ($o$ ranks $x$ above $y$). An alternative $t$ is top-ranked by $o$ when $t \succ_o b$ for every alternative $b \ne t$.
nodes.title: Top-ranked alternative

nodes.summary: The relation of a strict total order $T$ on a type $\alpha$ is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$, which is irreflexive, transitive, and relates any two distinct elements in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Relation of a strict preference order

nodes.summary: A binary relation $<$ on a type $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$ whose relation is $<$.
nodes.title: Building a strict preference order in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting

nodes.summary: For a type $A$ of alternatives and a type $V$ of voters, a profile is a function assigning to each voter $i \in V$ a strict total order $\lt _i$ on $A$, the strict preference of voter $i$.
nodes.title: Preference profiles for the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: For a type $A$ of alternatives and a type $V$ of voters, a resolute social choice function is a function $F$ sending each profile $p$ (an assignment of a strict total order on $A$ to each voter in $V$) to a single chosen alternative $F(p) \in A$.
nodes.title: Social choice functions

nodes.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ is a binary relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). In the Gibbard–Satterthwaite development it models a voter's strict preference over alternatives.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b \in \alpha$ and $a \ne b$, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.
nodes.title: Strict preferences in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting are total

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of strict preferences in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
